title: Curios of the Week #184
author: Greg Ashman
summary: In this bumper, PISA-themed edition of his weekly roundup, Ashman documents and adjudicates a live public argument over how to interpret the newly released PISA 2025 results. He recounts writing an EducationHQ op-ed (after a newspaper editor who solicited a pitch went silent) arguing that Finland's education system, long held up as a model, has continued declining because 'Finland appears to have learned from the educationalists' rather than the reverse. He then rebuts a LinkedIn response from Adam Voigt, who pointed to Ireland's PISA reading score as evidence for community-based, equity-first schooling; Ashman counters that Ireland's reading lead over England is not statistically significant, that Ireland's scores are trending down across all three PISA domains, and that England has actually pulled ahead of Ireland in science and mathematics. A separate section catches Pasi Sahlberg, author of Finnish Lessons, making a factual error in a media interview by claiming every OECD country hit an all-time low in 2025, which Ashman shows is false using Turkey as a counterexample, while also correcting his own earlier claim about Finland vs. Australia's science scores. The piece closes by noting the muted UK government reaction to England's relatively strong results under new Education Secretary Lucy Powell.
points: Ashman argues Finland's continued PISA decline shows the country adopted the very progressive 'educationalist' reforms that made its earlier success a global model, inverting the usual moral of the Finland story.

He rebuts Adam Voigt's claim that Ireland's reading score beats England's, noting the two scores (500 vs. 497) are not statistically significantly different and that Ireland is declining across all three PISA domains while England has pulled ahead in science and maths.
He documents a factual error by Pasi Sahlberg (author of Finnish Lessons), who told SBS News every OECD country hit an all-time low in 2025 -- disproven by Turkey's data.
Ashman publicly corrects his own earlier EducationHQ claim, acknowledging Finland's science score gap with Australia is not statistically significant after all, while its reading and maths gaps are.

The piece notes UK Education Secretary Lucy Powell's muted response to England's comparatively strong PISA showing, reading it as reluctance to credit the explicit-teaching approach that produced the result.
quotes: We were told these tales with breathless reforming zeal. And yet, instead of educationalists learning lessons from Finland, Finland appears to have learned from the educationalists and is doing worse as a result.
Claiming that Ireland's reading score is higher than England's is true but a little misleading. At 500, Ireland's score is not statistically significantly higher than England's 497.
Moreover, England's scores in science and mathematics used to be comparable with Ireland's, but England is now significantly ahead of Ireland in these subjects following Ireland's decline.
The truth is every country in the OECD is showing all-time-low results in everything. Very few countries were able to improve their results in 2025,
What is breathtaking is the contrast between Hargreaves' wide-eyed enthusiasm for Finland and a desperate search for something—anything—to explain the English results away.
